findings.text: The inode object represents a filesystem object with identity, ownership, times, size and block accounting plus links to operations, superblock and page cache. It carries mode, operation flags, general flags, user and group ids, operation vectors for inode and file, superblock and mapping pointers, inode number, link count exposed read only, device number, size, access modification and change timestamps with seconds and nanoseconds, generation, small byte count, block bits, write hint and block count. Synchronization uses a spinlock and a read write semaphore with ordered size handling where configured. Bookkeeping includes state flags, dirty times, hash node, IO list, writeback list, LRU and superblock lists, dentry hash or RCU head, version and sequence counters, reference and IO counters, lock context, embedded address space, device or link unions, and optional security, ACL, notification and private pointers.

The open file object tracks a single open instance with locking, access mode, operation vector, cache mapping, private data, inode link, open flags, IO control flags, credentials and signal ownership. It embeds a path that is logically constant, a position lock for regular files and directories sharing storage with pipe state, and a current offset. Error sequencing covers writeback and superblock errors, with optional poll structures. A trailing union shares task work, lockless list node, readahead state and deferred free pointer, followed by a reference count. The layout notes cache line boundaries and requests randomized layout with at least four byte alignment.
The file handle is a variable length identifier for export and lookup by handle, carrying a byte length, an integer type and a trailing byte array whose extent is described by the length field.

Readahead state records a window start and size, asynchronous size, page budget, access order, mmap miss count and previous position, allowing the filesystem and VM to decide sequential and random behavior.

Signal ownership for asynchronous IO records a back pointer to the owning file, a read write lock guarding identity fields, a target process or process group with its type, user and effective user ids, and a realtime signal number to deliver.

Asynchronous notification entries form a singly linked list per file, each holding a read write lock, a magic discriminator, a descriptor number, a next link, an owning file pointer and an RCU head for deferred reclamation. The magic constant has value hex 4601.

Directory iteration uses a callback type that consumes a context, name, length, offset and inode number, plus a context carrying the callback, current position, a caller supplied count hint and a mask of directory type flag bits the callback understands. Filesystems must not modify the count hint.
Rename arguments bundle the mount identity mapping, old and new parent dentries, old and new dentries, an optional delegated inode for lease break handling, and a flags word, with randomized layout.

File behavior is provided through a large operation vector covering seek, read and write in plain and vector forms, poll completion, shared directory iteration, polling, native and compatibility control, mapping and mapping preparation, open, flush, release, sync, async notification setup, record locking, unmapped area allocation, flag checking, BSD locking, splice read write and end of file, lease setting, preallocation, descriptor info display, copy and remap ranges, advice and uring command submission and polling, plus owner and capability flags. The table requests randomized layout.

Inode behavior is provided through a cache aligned operation vector covering lookup, symbolic link resolution, permission and ACL query, link target read, creation, hard link, unlink, symlink, directory creation and removal, special node creation, rename, attribute set and get, extended attribute listing, extent mapping, time update and lazy time sync, atomic open, temporary unnamed file creation, ACL set, file attribute set and get, and offset context retrieval. Time update distinguishes access time from combined change and modification handling.

A filesystem type registers a name, a flags word, a context initialization callback, an optional parameter table, a superblock destruction callback, an owner module, list linkage, a list of live superblocks, and dedicated lock class keys for superblock lock, unmount, rename, per freeze level writers, inode spinlock, inode mutex, invalidate lock and directory mutex.

Inode state is wrapped in a small structure holding one enumeration value, isolating state from other inode fields. Directory and inode mutex ordering uses named subclasses for normal, parent, child, extended attribute, second non directory and second parent cases.

Inode lifetime and writeback progress are tracked by bit numbers for new, syncing and LRU isolation, with one bit position reserved for wait addressing, and a wider flag set for dirty sync, dirty datasync, dirty pages, will free, freeing, clear, referenced, linkable, dirty time, writeback switch, overlay in use, creating, do not cache, sync queued, pinning network writeback and metadata writeback. New and syncing and isolation occupy the low positions while the remaining flags occupy higher positions.

Dirty aggregates are defined by combination: the inode dirty aggregate combines sync and datasync dirty; the general dirty aggregate adds dirty pages to the inode aggregate; the all dirty aggregate adds dirty time to the general aggregate.

Inode general flags assign successive powers of two from bit zero through bit twelve for synchronous writes, no access time, append only, immutable, dead directory, no quota, directory synchronous, no change or modification time, swap file pinning, filesystem private, integrity metadata, automount referral and no security attributes. Direct access uses bit thirteen when enabled and zero when disabled. Higher bits cover encrypted, casefolded, verity, kernel internal file and anonymous inode, with one intermediate position unused in the routed text.
Unmount and mount control bits use hex one for force, hex two for detach only, hex four for expiry, hex eight for no symlink following, and hex eight hundred million for a guaranteed unused bit.

File operation capability flags occupy bits zero through eight for buffered read async, buffered write async, mapping synchronized, direct IO parallel write, huge page support, unsigned offset handling, asynchronous locking, do not cache and immutable file behavior.

No MMU mapping modes use hex one for copy and hex eight for direct, with read write and execute permissions borrowed from virtual memory may flags and a combined mask combining those three. Remap uses bit zero for dedup and bit one for shorten allowed, with the advisory alias equal to shorten allowed. Copy by splice uses bit zero. Directory fill control uses hex one thousand for no interrupt. Change time queried uses bit thirty one of a thirty two bit word. Compatibility pointer control is a null default.

Non large file size caps at two to the thirty first power minus one. Large file size has two build variants, one derived from unsigned long maximum shifted by page shift and one equal to signed long long maximum. Offset maxima are the type maxima for file offset types. Lock ownership is an opaque pointer type.

Filesystem type flags use values one, two, four, eight, sixteen, thirty two, sixty four, one hundred twenty eight, two hundred fifty six, five hundred twelve, one thousand twenty four, two thousand forty eight and thirty two thousand seven hundred sixty eight for requiring a device, binary mount data, subtype support, user namespace mount, disallowing notify permission, allowing identity mapping, multigrain time, large block size, power freeze, restricted user namespace mount, delegatable user namespace mount, no notification marks and internal handling of dentry move during rename.

Shared inode locking takes the inode read write semaphore in read mode with a caller supplied subclass for lock ordering. Address space invalidation uses a separate read write semaphore with exclusive lock and unlock, shared lock and unlock, and a nonblocking shared attempt returning success or failure.

The inode spinlock guards block count, byte count and possibly size, and is held while setting the metadata writeback state. File signal ownership uses a read write lock guarding process identity and user fields. Async notification entries carry their own read write lock.

Link count is not written directly by filesystems; helpers adjust it and the increment path also marks the inode dirty. An inode is considered dirty time only when its sampled state contains exactly the dirty time bit among the set also testing new, freeing and will free.

Superblock based predicates test read only and mandatory locking via the superblock flags, while inode based predicates test no quota, private, integrity metadata and whiteout by mode and device. Cached symlink setup requires length consistency and absence of a prior cached link, then stores pointer and length and sets the cached flag. Fake hashing marks an inode hash node as fake for anonymous use.

Readahead membership reports whether an index falls inside the window from start for size pages. Owner identifiers are read through user namespace conversion helpers. Attribute updates for user and group are needed only when the attribute is valid and the mapped identity differs from the current inode identity.
Access, modification and change time setters each build a timestamp from seconds and nanoseconds inputs and delegate to the corresponding timestamp install helper, returning the installed value.

Whiteout creation delegates to special node creation with character device mode plus whiteout mode and a reserved device number. Mapping preparation delegates to the file operation vector. Device numbers are split into major and minor components via helpers.

Extension points for filesystems are the file operation vector, the inode operation vector and the filesystem type descriptor with its context setup and superblock teardown callbacks and parameter specification.

Storing a cached symbolic link target without length validation or with double caching triggers warnings. Treating the link count field as writable, modifying directory iteration count, or confusing exclusive and shared invalidation locking can corrupt state. Whiteout relies on a reserved device number and character mode that must not collide with real devices.
